headline: 485 chemicals in US pesticides linked to breast cancer, study finds
summary: New research identifies hundreds of chemicals in common pesticide products, including "inert" ingredients, that are associated with breast cancer as early-onset rates surge globally.
details: A peer-reviewed paper published in Environmental Health Perspectives reveals that at least 485 chemicals found in US pesticide products are linked to breast cancer. This finding raises significant concerns about the safety of food and everyday products, especially amid a global rise in early-onset breast cancer.

The study highlights regulatory deficiencies in the US, noting that the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) often overlooks "inert" ingredients, which are not subjected to rigorous safety reviews. These chemicals are present not only in agricultural pesticides but also in consumer products like lice treatments and flea repellents.

Breast cancer incidence has been increasing by 1% annually in the US, with a faster rise observed in women under 50. Concurrently, pesticide use has grown, and federal data indicates that 84 of the identified breast cancer-linked chemicals are present in the general population, though scientists believe this is an undercount.

The research points out that the chemical industry may be exploiting the "inert" status to avoid health scrutiny. These ingredients, often added to enhance pesticide effectiveness, are not biologically inert and pose significant health risks, including cancer, even at low exposure levels.

Public health advocates are calling for stronger regulations, such as expanding California's Proposition 65 to include more chemicals known to cause harm. They also criticize the EPA's approach to hormone-disrupting chemicals and the influence of industry lobbyists on regulatory decisions.

Consumers can take protective measures by opting for organic produce and products treated with fewer pesticides. Resources are available to help identify produce with lower pesticide residues, offering a way to mitigate exposure.
